questions.title: Enzyme's substrate-binding surface
questions.question: In contrast to inorganic catalysts, enzymes have an intricately shaped surface called the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A cofactor is a non-protein helper molecule or metal ion an enzyme may require for activity; it is not the intricately shaped binding surface itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The substrate is the molecule the enzyme acts on, not the shaped surface of the enzyme that binds it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The apoenzyme is the protein portion of an enzyme that requires a cofactor to become catalytically active (the holoenzyme); it is not specifically the name for the intricately shaped binding surface.
explanations.D: Correct. The active site is the enzyme's intricately shaped surface, a three-dimensional pocket or cleft formed by the folded protein. It binds the substrate with high specificity and carries out catalysis. This precisely shaped binding surface, tailored by the protein's fold to one substrate or a narrow family of substrates, is exactly what distinguishes an enzyme's specificity from the far less selective action of a simple inorganic catalyst.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the active site as the enzyme's intricately shaped substrate-binding and catalytic surface.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Active site", p28
